A.explanation: The aeroplane climbs at a steady rate, so its velocity is constant and the resultant force on it can be zero.

B.explanation: The glider can move in a straight line at constant velocity at constant altitude, so thrust, drag, lift and weight can balance.

C.explanation: Changing direction changes velocity even at constant speed, so the speedboat accelerates and must have a non-zero resultant force.

D.explanation: The ship can be towed steadily in a straight line, so the two tow forces plus drag can give zero resultant force.

hints: Focus on the underlined body and check whether both its speed and its direction of motion stay unchanged.
Recall that equilibrium needs zero resultant force, so by Newton's first law the velocity vector $v$ must stay constant.
Contrast steady climb and constant-altitude towing with changes direction at a constant speed to find where acceleration is unavoidable.
walkthrough: Recall the condition for equilibrium: the resultant force $F$ on the body must be zero, so $F = ma = 0$.
That means acceleration $a$ must be zero, so the velocity vector must be constant in both magnitude and direction.
A steady climb in a straight line and straight-line motion at constant altitude both have constant velocity, so zero resultant force is possible.
A towed ship can also move into harbour steadily in a straight line, so its tow forces and resistance can balance.
Changing direction at constant speed still changes velocity because velocity is a vector, so the body has acceleration towards the centre of the turn.
Accelerated motion needs a non-zero resultant force, so equilibrium is impossible for the speedboat that changes direction. This is option C
